title: Collard greens
subtitle: Slow-braised Southern greens with ham hock and vinegar
excerpt: Collard greens are thick, dark leaves from the brassica family braised for 1.5 to 2 hours with a ham hock, onion, garlic, and chicken stock. Long cooking collapses the tough leaves into silky, yielding bites. A splash of cider vinegar at the end cuts the richness. The cooking liquid, called pot liquor, is considered the best part.
sourceNotes: Southern American culinary tradition. Slow-cooked greens with smoked pork are central to soul-food cooking and documented in Edna Lewis, The Taste of Country Cooking (1976). The tradition has West African roots; collard greens were a staple crop in the American South from the seventeenth century onwards.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in the cooking liquid for up to 3 months. The greens soften further on reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. The greens improve overnight in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 3 days ahead. Reheat gently in the pot with a splash of stock.

glossaryTerms.definition: The cooking liquid left in the pot after braising collard greens or other Southern greens. Rich in flavour from the ham, aromatics, and the greens themselves, it is drunk from the bowl or sopped up with cornbread.

content.text: Collard greens are braised slowly in stock with a smoked ham hock until the tough leaves become tender and silky. The long cook extracts gelatin from the ham hock and flavour from both the pork and the greens, giving a dark, rich
. Cider vinegar and a pinch of chilli flakes added at the end sharpen the whole thing.

items.prepNote: collard greens or cavolo nero, leaves stripped from stems

content.text: Put the {{ham-hock}} ham hock, {{onion}} onion, and {{garlic}} of garlic in the Dutch oven. Pour over {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock and add enough water to cover the hock by a few centimetres. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for 45 minutes.

Strip the {{spring-greens}} of collard or spring greens leaves from their thick stems. Cut or tear into large pieces. Add to the pot in batches, pushing them down as they wilt. Add the chilli flakes if using. Simmer covered for a further 45 minutes to 1 hour until completely tender.

Lift out the ham hock. Pull the meat from the bone, shred it, and return it to the pot. Discard the bone. Add {{cider-vinegar}} of cider vinegar and black pepper. Taste and adjust. Serve in bowls with the pot liquor, alongside cornbread. Hot sauce is on the table.

items.cause: Heat too gentle, or collard greens are particularly thick.
items.fix: Keep simmering. Some batches of collard greens need the full 1.5 hours to become silky. Keep the lid on.

items.cause: Ham hock very salty, or seasoning added before tasting.
items.fix: Taste before adding any extra salt. Most smoked ham hocks provide enough salt on their own.

items.cause: Greens cooked without enough liquid, or cavolo nero used without the longer cook.
items.fix: Keep the greens submerged during cooking. Cavolo nero needs the full time. The vinegar at the end also helps to balance any bitterness.

content.text: Mustard greens or turnip greens can be used in the same way, with a shorter cooking time of 30 to 45 minutes. A vegetarian version replaces the ham hock with smoked paprika, a teaspoon of liquid smoke if available, and vegetable stock. Cavolo nero is the closest British substitute for collard greens and works well in this method.

Collard greens are a cornerstone of the American soul-food tradition, with West African roots and a history tied to the cooking of enslaved people in the American South. The tradition of slow-cooking greens with smoked pork and drinking the pot liquor is one of the oldest cooking practices in American history. Served with cornbread, black-eyed peas, and sweet potato, they make the classic soul-food plate.
